name: Insensitivity to sample size
statement: People judge how likely a sample result is without much regard for how large the sample was, though the failure belongs to a particular kind of question rather than to reasoning in general.
meaning: The variability of a sample statistic falls as the sample grows, so an extreme result is more likely in a small sample than in a large one. Kahneman and Tversky argued that people do not use this. Their account is that a sample result is judged by how far it resembles the population it came from, and resemblance has no size in it. The parent mechanism has its own entry here, under representativeness heuristic, along with its replication record and the dispute over whether it is defined tightly enough to test. What is at issue here is the specific error, which the 1974 review lists as one of six. The demonstration everyone knows is the hospital problem: two hospitals, one with about 45 births a day and one with about 15, and a question about which recorded more days on which more than 60% of babies were boys. The smaller hospital is the answer. Reading the pattern as a general blindness to sample size is what the later literature will not support.

origin.note: The hospital problem appears in "Subjective Probability: A Judgment of Representativeness", which Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer place at page 443. The 1974 Science review carries the version that is quoted, and the counts quoted with it. The 1972 paper could not be opened during this check, so figures attributed to it here come from the supplement to the 2025 replication.

evidence: The 1974 review states the case in a paragraph. Told that a larger hospital delivers about 45 babies a day and a smaller one about 15, and asked which recorded more days on which more than 60% of babies were boys, 21 undergraduates chose the larger, 21 the smaller and 53 said about the same, within 5 percent of each other. The review adds that this notion of statistics "is evidently not part of people's repertoire of intuitions". Two other results sit beside it. Asked which sample argued more strongly that an urn was mostly red, 4 red out of 5 drawn or 12 red out of 20, most people picked the first, though the correct posterior odds are 8 to 1 and 16 to 1. Asked for the probability that average height in a sample exceeds 6 feet, subjects gave the same answer for samples of 1,000, 100 and 10. The review also reports a study of experienced research psychologists whose statistical intuitions showed a belief in what it calls the law of small numbers, leaving them putting too much faith in small samples and overestimating how well such results would repeat. The design behind the hospital counts is not in the review. The supplement to the 2025 replication reports that problems 7 to 9 went to Stanford undergraduates with no background in probability or statistics, split across two versions, one asking about days above 60% and one about days below it. In the first, 12 chose the larger hospital, 10 the smaller and 28 the same. In the second, where the larger hospital is the correct answer, 9 chose the larger, 11 the smaller and 25 the same. The supplement puts 97 participants in the two versions together and prints counts totalling 95.

replication.headline: The preregistered replication reproduced the low rate of correct answers on the hospital problem and not its direction, and rewording the same question raises correct answers from a median of 33% to 76%.
replication.detail: Mayiwar, Wan, Løhre and Feldman ran the first direct replication of the 1972 paper, on 623 participants recruited on Amazon MTurk through CloudResearch, each taking five of the nine problems. The hospital problem went to 346 of them, 173 per version. Where the question asked about days above 60%, 52 chose the smaller hospital, which is correct, 50 the larger and 71 about the same. Where it asked about days below 60%, 54 chose the larger, which is correct there, 48 the smaller and 71 about the same. The preregistered test compared the rate of correct answers against the 33.33% expected by chance across three options. It found nothing in either version: p = .798, Cohen's h = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.08], and p = .695, h = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.10]. Their recomputation of the 1972 data gives h = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.03] and h = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.60, -0.01], so the original sat further below chance than the replication did. Both versions are coded in their table as no signal, inconsistent, smaller. The paper nevertheless counts the problem as successfully replicated, on the ground that the number choosing the correct answer did not exceed 50%, and it quotes Teigen's objection that comparing the correct answer against "equally likely" forms no testable null. Two other lines matter. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer separated tasks that ask about a distribution of sample means from tasks that ask about one sample, and sorted 35 studies from eight articles by that distinction. Correct choices ran from 7% to 59% on the first kind, median 33%, and from 56% to 87% on the second, median 76%. Chance is 33% when there are three options. Bishop, Thompson and Parker put the incentive and training question to a registered report with in-principle acceptance on 12 August 2021. Their 100 participants had studied life or social science for at least a term, were recruited through Prolific and social media, and were paid a bonus for each correct answer. On the six sample-size items of the pre-training quiz the mean score was 1.7 in the first sample and 1.96 in the second, against a test value of 5, p < .001 in both, and two participants in 100 scored 5 or more. Training on a task that showed data points accumulating did raise earnings on that task, combined Bayes factor 164.222, and did not move the quiz: the pre-post term in their mixed model came out at 0.015 with a standard error of 0.019.

study.cite: Mayiwar, L., Wan, K. H., Løhre, E., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting representativeness heuristic classic paradigms: Replication and extensions of nine experiments in Kahneman and Tversky (1972). Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 78(4), 707-730.

limits: The wording carries the result. Murray, Iding, Farris and Revlin gave the hospital problem to 69 undergraduates at three birth-rate ratios. At the original 45 against 15, 7.1% answered correctly and 92.9% said about the same. At 50 against 5 the figures were 20.7% and 51.7%, and at 1,000 against 5 they were 30.7% and 42.3%. The fall in the same answer was reliable, F(2, 66) = 5.4, p < .01, while the gain in accuracy across their two problems reached only F(2, 132) = 2.6, p = .08, and the authors state that the salience manipulation did not produce significantly greater accuracy on the hospital problem. Weixler, Sommerhoff and Ufer put several variants to 242 mathematics teacher education students and report that a larger deviation from the expected relative frequency and a larger ratio between the two sample sizes both raise solution rates, that the effects of task features weaken after the first task, and that a task phrased around a 100% frequency helps students with later ones. Their body text is behind a paywall and only the abstract was read, at Springer and at ERIC, so no solution rate from that study is quoted here. The 1972 paper itself stayed shut, and its counts here are the replication supplement's reading of it. No multi-site or multi-laboratory replication of the hospital problem was located in Crossref, Europe PMC, the Open Science Framework or the Many Labs and Registered Replication Report catalogues. No study was located that varied the size of a monetary incentive on a sample-size problem; the incentive evidence here is Bishop and colleagues' flat bonus per correct answer. A registered replication of the 1971 paper on research psychologists received a Stage 1 recommendation from Moin Syed at Peer Community in Registered Reports on 19 June 2023, and a Crossref search returned no Stage 2 report.
misreadings: The famous counts are real and they are not what they look like. The 21, 21 and 53 come from the 1974 Science review, which prints one question, the version about days above 60%, and one undistinguished set of 95 responses. The 1972 study behind them ran two versions with opposite correct answers. Add the supplement's two sets of counts together and they give 21, 21 and 53 exactly, which is arithmetic done here rather than a claim either paper makes. If that is what happened, then 9 of the 21 people filed under the wrong answer had answered the mirrored question correctly. Second, the problem is routinely sourced to the 1974 review. It is from the 1972 paper, and the review is a summary of work published elsewhere. Third, about the same is described as what people say, and in the replication it was chosen by 71 of 173 in each version, a plurality rather than a majority. Fourth, and the one that matters, the result is quoted as showing that people ignore sample size. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer's sorting puts the median at 33% correct on questions about the spread of sample means and 76% on questions about a single sample, and their reading is that intuition tracks the plain idea that bigger samples estimate better, which the hospital problem does not reward. Fifth, this is not base-rate neglect and not scope insensitivity, both of which have their own entries. Sixth, the headline that eight of nine problems replicated covers a problem whose own directional test found nothing in either version, and whose verdict rests on correct answers staying under half.
